episode_thesis: Carver argues trend following is a risk premium rather than an edge (anyone can do it, so the pay is compensation for discomfort), and that a systematic trader survives by keeping costs low, leverage moderate and avoiding overfitting: build backtests as rolling, past-only selection across many strategies, size positions by dynamic volatility targeting (the skew gained from not scaling does not repay the Sharpe lost), and trade slowly. On the total portfolio approach adopted by CalPERS he is hopeful but sceptical: judging a CTA by its contribution to the whole portfolio should help diversifiers, but the approach has no formal definition.

speakers.name: Rob Carver
speakers.role: independent systematic futures trader, author of Systematic Trading, ex-AHL (Man Group)
speakers.speaker_note: Captions have no labels but host questions are read in a distinct style and Carver's answers are first-person about his own system, blog and AHL experience. The ledger correction moves the Bitcoin halving remark (C05) to Carver; the host's joke about being 'hot' follows. In C16 Carver cannot recall the author of an execution paper (probably AQR, he says).

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following is a risk premium, not an edge: if anyone with capital and a spreadsheet can do it, the profit must be compensation for taking risks others find uncomfortable. The two main explanations are psychological biases and delayed reaction to information.
worldview_premises.support: first-principles argument; a recent Cliff Asness podcast making the same point

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following works across many asset classes with long holding periods; it is not designed for single asset classes or fast speeds. Trend efficacy falls below holding periods of about one or two weeks to a month, and below about one hour mean reversion appears.
worldview_premises.support: his experience of how trend systems perform by holding period; no data shown

worldview_premises.premise: Three things kill systematic traders: excessive costs, excessive leverage and overfitting. His advice has not changed in 10-20 years; backtesting principles are not new scientific discoveries.
worldview_premises.support: about 20 years in the CTA industry; 11.5 years running his own automated platform

worldview_premises.premise: A backtest has two jobs, finding future strategies and estimating past performance. Selecting the best in-sample strategies destroys the second job because the result is selected on the same data; and picking the top few from many (multiple testing) selects luck.
worldview_premises.support: statistical argument: 10 of 1,000 flat strategies will look amazing by chance

worldview_premises.premise: Dynamic volatility sizing beats fixed sizing for geometric return: positive skew improves CAGR but hurts Sharpe, and the skew gained from not volatility-scaling does not compensate for the Sharpe lost. A high-Sharpe, less skewed system with a bit more leverage can beat the CAGR of high-skew, high-vol CTAs.
worldview_premises.support: theoretical result on his blog (not empirical) that assumes leverage can be adjusted

worldview_premises.premise: Upside and downside volatility are the same risk for sizing: returns are close to a coin flip, so a large position after a big rise is a coin flip away from becoming a large loss.
worldview_premises.support: reasoning; he says the question about asymmetric volatility is the one he has no real answer for

worldview_premises.premise: Third-party sentiment indicators and sell-side models are typically fitted in-sample and should be built in-house; skew, option ratios and the VIX level are valid sentiment proxies even though he does not use them.
worldview_premises.support: AHL experience of sell-side vendors; digging into construction

worldview_premises.premise: Strategic asset allocation is a top-down box structure that ignores correlation across boxes; a total portfolio approach evaluates additions holistically, which should favour diversifying strategies and help CTAs that fit neither the hedge-fund nor the tail-protection box.
worldview_premises.support: his work with allocators and multi-manager groups at Man Group; a made-up Danish equities example

worldview_premises.premise: Capacity-limited alpha stays inside: Renaissance's closed Medallion fund returns differ massively from its outside funds, possibly because good ideas are kept inside or have limited capacity.
worldview_premises.support: public returns of Renaissance's outside funds, including a CTA-type fund that underperformed

mechanism_chains.fails_when: Very short time frames, where there is enough data to separate strategies; Monte Carlo and holdout tests help but do not fix selection of a tiny subset on too little data.

decision_process.practice: Match backtest data frequency to holding period: tick data only for fast strategies, none for monthly holding; test a one-day execution delay and expect no material change for slow systems.
decision_process.why: a slow strategy insensitive to a one-day delay need not trade at the close

decision_process.practice: Do not build on 3-5 years of data for a monthly-holding system; include trading costs from the start and drop any strategy that does not make money before slippage.
decision_process.why: insufficient data for calibration; costs belong in the design

decision_process.practice: Refit strategy weights about annually for monthly-holding systems (AHL did); personally about every three years, usually when other changes are made.
decision_process.why: an extra year adds under 2% to 55 years of data

decision_process.practice: Continuous dynamic position sizing on volatility, trend strength and possibly account size; no stop losses and no ATR, with risk handled by standard-deviation sizing.
decision_process.why: better geometric return than fixed sizing, theory

decision_process.practice: Trade through the day after the previous close (not at the close); institutional size should spread trades through the day; run the dynamic optimiser through the day only with care about reacting to intraday bounces.
decision_process.why: performance lies between trading at the previous and next close; reduces market impact

decision_process.practice: Buffering or smoothing instead of daily rebalancing.
decision_process.why: avoids churn on noisy volatility estimates

decision_process.practice: Skew signal: buy assets with heavy negative historic skew, which tend to be underpriced because people dislike them.
decision_process.why: a form of buying negative sentiment; he uses no other sentiment indicators

decision_process.practice: Use monthly, weekly or daily data to estimate Sharpe and volatility; use daily data for ATR/volatility estimates, weekly systems can be tested on weekly data.
decision_process.why: annual returns hide autocorrelation that biases annualised Sharpe and volatility; more frequent data gives more accurate volatility

decision_process.practice: Idea in his back book: execute slow signals the next day only if price has moved in your favour (buy only after a dip), combining slow trend with short-term mean reversion for cheaper execution.
decision_process.why: better fills from a fast mean-reversion element without extra trades; untested for delays over one day

speakers.evidence_style: First principles and statistics (multiple testing, skew-Sharpe theory, autocorrelation), his own long backtests (data from 1970) and blog articles, and AHL practice; explicit about what is theory versus empirical and about what he has not tested.

current_views.view: His own risk sizing is below average, consistent with a neutral trend barometer; he is up about 5% for the year, in a drawdown of just over 10% (about 3% below mid-October), with the largest short in Bitcoin and net long equities (short DAX, long Italy).
current_views.reasoning: the system, not his opinion, drives positions; trends have become more volatile since September-October

CalPERS' move to a total portfolio approach could help trend following, but he suspects it is partly an excuse to add more private assets; he calls it hopeful but vague.

current_views.reasoning: obligations to retirees put investment risk on the manager

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
speakers.role: host, Top Traders Unplugged; CTA background
speakers.speaker_note: Host. He reads listener questions and states views on 2025 CTA performance, ETFs, trend decay and total portfolio approach. The ledger correction reassigns the Bitcoin halving remark to Carver.

worldview_premises.premise: Apparent decay in trend following mainly reflects poor market environments over the last 20 years, which research teams cannot overcome, not a broken strategy; success needs commitment to the rules and comfort with a strategy that is unpredictable day to day but predictable in the long run.
Trend systems have evolved without changing core rules: more differentiation of speeds between entry and exit signals, and better risk management and use of volatility.

In 2025 differences between CTAs, ETFs and replicators came from exposure (how much equity, fixed income) and market universe rather than model type, so conclusions about which approach is better are dangerous; a fund with a low-equity-correlation mandate should not be judged against the S&P 500.
worldview_premises.support: performance comparison and a Renaissance product mandate

worldview_premises.premise: Allocators chase past performance with too short a horizon (a Midwestern pension added CTAs after 2022 and was disappointed), and cheaper ETFs drew inflows after outperforming in 2025.
worldview_premises.support: a trade press article on a pension fund; ETF flows

worldview_premises.premise: Even elite quant funds suffer outlier months, so a single large monthly loss reported by a journalist (Renaissance equity funds) is a selected number; the Renaissance outside equity fund lost 19% in 2022 and returned only 3.7% since inception.
worldview_premises.support: fund returns recalled from an article

worldview_premises.premise: CalPERS' move to a total portfolio approach (from July 2026, reference portfolio 75% equities/25% bonds) makes trend following more interesting because each component will be judged by its contribution to the portfolio.
worldview_premises.support: the board vote and quoted statements

disagreements.topic: How much has trend following changed in 20 years?

positions.speaker: Rob Carver
positions.position: His advice and principles have not changed in 10-20 years.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Entry rules are unchanged but risk management, volatility use and speed differentiation between entry and exit have evolved.

disagreements.topic: Is the total portfolio approach good news for trend following?

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Very interesting for trend, since each component is judged by its contribution to the portfolio.

positions.speaker: Rob Carver
positions.position: Holistic thinking should help diversifiers, but he is sceptical: vague, management-consultant language and maybe an excuse for more private assets; a formal definition from big quant allocators would be a game-changer.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Carver's static-versus-dynamic result is theoretical and he stresses it is not an empirical result; his claim that extra leverage on a high-Sharpe system beats high-skew CTAs rests on that theory and on being able to lever without limit.
The rolling selection backtest is described as the gold standard but not demonstrated; costs of implementing it with many strategies and the choice of weighting scheme are not discussed.
Skew as sentiment: the ledger correction notes Carver only says one could argue it; his rule buys heavy negative skew, which he says tends to be underpriced, without evidence given.
Carver cannot answer the asymmetric-volatility question empirically and offers only a coin-flip argument for treating upside and downside volatility alike.
The execute-only-after-a-favourable-move idea is untested and may lose trend capture if fills are delayed by more than one day.
The Renaissance comparison mixes outside funds with the closed Medallion fund; the explanations (capacity, ideas kept inside) are guesses.
The host's view that decay reflects environment and not strategy is offered without a test; Carver's risk premium argument is compatible with either.

Carver reports a heated disagreement with people on X who claim a moving-average crossover is an edge, but the counter-arguments are not presented, so his edge-versus-risk-premium view is one-sided in this episode.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Observable inputs the speakers treat as leading performance: the trend barometer and the size of market moves for trend returns; the volatility estimate used for sizing (with EWMA smoothing); market universe and equity or fixed income exposure for product differences; correlations for fixed-vol-target systems; formal publications by large quant allocators (ADIA) for the total portfolio approach. Horizons: monthly holding period and annual or multi-year refits for the strategy; July 2026 for CalPERS' switch.
reader_inferences: Carver's advice on backtests implies that published CTA-style backtests that select a small share of many candidates on a few years of data overstate expected performance.

His risk premium framing, plus the claim that trend efficacy falls below about a month, suggests lower-speed signals carry the premium and costs eat the faster ones; it is consistent with the host's view that short lookbacks are poor.

If the TPA is adopted and judged holistically, a CTA's correlation to an allocator's other holdings (not only its stand-alone Sharpe) becomes the selling point; this favours CTAs with low equity beta.
Carver's theory result on skew versus Sharpe implies that, for a given CAGR target, an allocator choosing between a high-skew CTA and a high-Sharpe CTA should consider the leverage they can apply.
